title: Same answers, two verdicts
topic: the halo effect: why a first impression changes how we judge everything after it
hook: Same person. Same answers. Two completely different interviews.
promise: One visible trait colours how we judge everything else about a person (the halo effect).

takeaway.text: Before you judge an answer, ask whether you already judged the person.

scenes.narration: Same person. Same answers. Two completely different interviews.
scenes.visualIdea: Two doors, the same candidate walks through both: once in a wrinkled hoodie, once in a suit.

scenes.narration: Alex walks in, hands over his CV and answers every question well. The interviewer nods politely and writes almost nothing.
scenes.visualIdea: Alex walks in, in a hoodie, hands his CV across the desk. Maria barely looks up and keeps typing.

scenes.narration: Now the same Alex walks in wearing a suit. Same CV, same answers. This time she leans in and fills the page.
scenes.visualIdea: The same scene again: Alex in a suit. Maria leans forward, smiles, takes notes.

scenes.narration: Psychologists call this the halo effect. One thing we notice first spills over onto everything else.
scenes.visualIdea: Over Alex's head a soft glow appears that only the interviewer seems to see.

scenes.narration: The suit did not make him smarter. It changed what she was looking for.
scenes.visualIdea: Her notes: on one side 'smart, reliable, a leader', on the other almost blank.

scenes.narration: So next time an answer impresses you, ask what you saw before you heard it.
scenes.visualIdea: Alex alone, in neither outfit, looking at the viewer.

claims.text: Edward Thorndike described the halo effect in 1920 after studying how officers rated soldiers.
claims.role: gives the effect its origin and name
